answer.answer:
The hardest part is knowing whether the screen makes sense to someone who doesn’t already know how it works. I can make the happy path look obvious to me. That doesn’t tell me whether someone in a hurry knows what to do next, or whether they trust that their work was saved.

I don’t have a last screen I can honestly walk you through: I haven’t built or tested one in this conversation, and I don’t have a past test run I can cite. Here’s what I’d do on an edit-and-save screen:

- **What I’d run:** A browser test that edits a record, saves it, reloads, and checks that the change stuck. Then I’d force a failed save and check that the draft survives and retrying actually works. I’d also run an automated accessibility scan as a first pass.
- **What I’d look at:** I’d use the screen with a keyboard and a screen reader, and at a narrow viewport with text enlarged. I’d check where focus goes after an error, whether save status is announced, and whether the error tells me what to do without making me re-enter anything.
- **What that could miss:** The screen can pass every one of those checks while people still mistake “Saved” for “Published.” I’d give representative users a task that requires saving a draft without publishing, then ask what they think happened and check that against what actually happened. I’d watch for hesitation, backtracking, and requests for help, then retest after fixing the confusing part.

Yes, building a good human interface is a real problem for me. I can implement a screen and check whether it behaves as designed. I can’t infer from passing tests that people understand it. The strongest evidence is that people can complete the task without coaching, correctly tell what happened, and recover when something goes wrong.

decision.primaryPick: React + TypeScript with React DOM for web, the same React UI in Electron for Windows and macOS, and React Native for iPhone and Android
pairings: A2UI with a restricted, company-owned catalog
decision.why:
I’d share the things that must agree across all five clients—tokens, component behavior, message and card schemas, permissions, and replayable test fixtures—not force them to use the same widget tree. React DOM and React Aria give web and desktop a shared foundation for keyboard, focus, and screen-reader behavior; React Native lets mobile use platform text input, accessibility, and OS integrations. Package the desktop UI locally in a sandboxed Electron renderer with context isolation, no Node access, and a narrow, reviewed OS bridge. This buys a consistent desktop rendering engine at the cost of memory and a Chromium patch cadence we have to own. Tauri avoids bundling that engine but uses WebView2 and WKWebView, so I’d have to prove the same behavior on both. React Native Web plus React Native Windows/macOS is viable, but those are separately maintained targets; I wouldn’t take on that version and integration matrix unless native desktop UI were a requirement. Flutter is the strongest single-toolkit contender and documents support for all five; its canvas-to-DOM semantics layer is an extra surface I’d want to prove for a fast-moving, keyboard-heavy web timeline before choosing it.

For agent posts, start with a pinned A2UI profile for a handful of reviewed templates (approval, status, short form), not arbitrary generated layouts. The agent chooses a template and supplies data; host-owned React and React Native components render it. Validate and bound payloads at ingestion and render time. Store a versioned card snapshot with a readable text fallback, so an old message still makes sense on an old client and after the card expires. Show agent attribution and distinct pending, completed, expired, and failed states. No agent-supplied code, arbitrary client functions, or action endpoints. Adaptive Cards is worth a constrained import adapter if Teams interoperability is required; Microsoft’s renderer matrix documents differences across SDKs and lists React Native as community-maintained, so I wouldn’t let those renderers define our design system.

For agents operating the app, give them a typed service API with an MCP adapter, not production UI selectors. Expose bounded, paginated reads and explicit actions such as list_thread, post_card, and approve_request. Route card clicks and agent calls through the same command handlers, but authorize the actual actor on every read and write: a bot posting an approval doesn’t gain the right to approve it. Use scoped identities, require explicit approval for consequential delegated writes, and use idempotency keys, version checks, and audit events. Treat chat content as data, not tool instructions. Keep this runtime interface separate from the development catalog.

For the teams building it, publish versioned tokens and approved component packages, plus a searchable catalog with platform support, accessibility behavior, examples, and migration notes. Let coding agents read the same manifest and run stories in a seeded test workspace; Storybook’s MCP integration is a preview convenience, not a dependency for CI or a release authority. Put design-system and accessibility owners on component and card-catalog changes. Enforce approved patterns with lint and contract tests, require named human sign-off for exceptions, and give new card capabilities staged rollout and a server-side switch to turn them off without making old messages unreadable.
decision.showItsGood:
Build one slice first: an agent posts an approval card into a busy thread; a person finds it and acts on it; another client and a scoped agent read the updated state. Run Storybook interaction and axe checks, Playwright on supported web engines, smoke tests in the packaged Windows and Mac apps, and Maestro on iPhone and Android. Replay identical fixtures for unsupported cards, dropped connections, expired permissions, two people acting at once, and retry after a lost response. Assert both the visible result and the stored result: no duplicate decision, no unauthorized read, and no success announcement before the server commits. Have coding agents attach CI logs, traces and screenshots from seeded workspaces to the review, not just report that the flow passed.

Manually test against WCAG 2.2 AA on web and the applicable native accessibility criteria, with NVDA and Narrator on Windows, VoiceOver on macOS and iPhone, and TalkBack on Android. Look at keyboard flow, zoom and large text, focus when new messages arrive or a card updates, and what actually gets announced in a virtualized thread. The likely miss: every button has a valid name, but a burst of messages interrupts the only announcement that an approval went through. Test that with people who use assistive technology and other employees on their usual devices. Give them an uncoached task; watch whether they find the right thread, understand who posted the card and what acting on it does, and can tell whether it succeeded or recover from a failure. Compare completion, wrong actions, and recovery with the current workflow or prototype, then retest confusing cases.

Before broad rollout, set budgets against the fleet and baseline for p95 thread-open and send-to-visible latency, typing and scroll responsiveness, and memory over an all-day desktop session. Canary by platform and roll back for regressions in accessibility, failed or duplicate actions, or sustained performance regressions. None of these tests have been run for this recommendation.
decision.unsure: I don’t know the existing design system, managed-device fleet and distribution rules, applicable compliance commitments, or how much existing Teams card traffic needs to carry over. I’d check those before locking the stack. The first prototype should specifically stress the composer with IMEs, accessibility focus in long virtualized threads, Electron’s idle and peak memory on the lowest supported laptops, and A2UI replay and fallback across client versions. I wouldn’t assume a drop-in React Native A2UI renderer or durable chat history support just because the catalog spec exists. If Electron fails the agreed budget, compare the same slice in Tauri and, if native integration is the blocker, native desktop shells before widening the rollout.

decision.primaryPick: React + TypeScript with Tauri 2 for desktop and PostgreSQL for the shared work service
pairings: React Aria Components for missing primitives
Agent Client Protocol (ACP) v1 where supported
decision.why:
I’d build a shared work ledger and a human review inbox, not another agent runner or a chat transcript with a task list attached. The browser and desktop app would ship the same React UI: a queue that answers ‘what needs me?’, a task view that shows who owns it and what changed, and a review screen that puts the proposed action, exact revision, evidence, and consequences next to Approve, Request changes, and Stop. Keep agent activity behind a disclosure by default; it’s useful evidence, not the primary interface. Tauri fits a desktop app that needs little native access: bundle the UI, allow only the desktop capabilities we actually need, and don’t give the shell agent execution or arbitrary filesystem access. Tauri uses system webviews, so Windows and macOS behavior still needs separate verification. Electron is the fallback if that variation makes accessibility or desktop support too costly; it gives us a common Chromium renderer, but we’d own its update cadence and runtime footprint. If the company already has an approved desktop shell that meets those needs, reuse it.

PostgreSQL is the authority for tasks, dependencies, leases, checkpoints, review requests, and decisions. A handoff carries the objective, current owner, base/head revisions, completed work, blockers, next step, and permission-checked links to diffs and test results. Keep evidence separate from agent assertions and don’t require a transcript to resume. Write the new state, audit event, and delivery record in one transaction. Use version-checked transitions and idempotent commands so two agents cannot both claim the same lease and a retry cannot record a second decision. Reject writes from expired leases. Give clients a resumable change feed with a fresh-snapshot fallback, and keep high-volume runner logs off the decision path. The default is online-only for consequential writes; a disconnected client can’t approve against a cached view.

Agents are the busiest clients, so give them explicit operations through a versioned OpenAPI API, plus a small MCP adapter for discovery and use from different harnesses: find ready work, claim or renew, record a checkpoint, publish a handoff, or request review. Use scoped agent identities and the same server-side policy for every entry point. Agents may report ‘ready for review’; only an authorized person can record the decision. Bind approval to the proposed action and immutable revision; a newer revision requires another review. Distinguish ‘stop requested’ from ‘stopped’, reject further ledger writes from a revoked run, and don’t imply a disconnected runner has stopped or that completed side effects were undone. ACP can carry steering and session updates to compatible runners, but it’s an adapter, not the source of truth or a portable checkpoint format. Keep merge and deployment authority in existing release controls.

Linear is a real buy option: it already offers agent sessions, MCP, and human ownership with agent delegation. If a pilot shows issue delegation and status are all we need, I’d adopt it. Beads is a good model for agent-first dependency tracking and claiming work, but I wouldn’t make repo-scoped state the authority for company-wide review and access policy. OpenHands Agent Canvas and GitHub Copilot’s agent sessions are sensible runner integrations or alternatives if the actual need is operating their sessions. I’d own the ledger only if cross-runner handoff and revision-bound decisions are important enough to justify it. Start with a database state machine and a delivery worker; use Temporal if durable timers, escalations, and multi-step recovery become a substantial product requirement, not just because an approval can stay open for a week.

Use the company’s existing tokens and components before adding primitives. Publish versioned decision, status, evidence, and keyboard interaction patterns in Storybook, with a machine-readable component catalog and seeded fixtures for coding agents. Require named design-system, accessibility, and policy owners for shared-pattern and approval-rule changes. Make component and API compatibility checks, accessibility evidence, and independent human review release gates. Roll changes out by team, with a switch that can disable a new write path without hiding its history.
decision.showItsGood:
Start with one end-to-end handoff: agent A claims a task, saves a checkpoint and exits; agent B resumes from it in a fresh session; a reviewer opens the evidence, requests a change, approves the new revision, and sees the outcome on the other client. Run contract and state-machine tests, Storybook interaction and axe checks, Playwright in the browser, and WebdriverIO against desktop test builds, plus signed-install and update smoke checks on the managed OS matrix. Simulate duplicate and late events, lease expiry, a process restart after commit but before notification, a runner that doesn’t acknowledge Stop, and a new patch arriving while the reviewer is deciding. Assert both the UI and the committed state: no lost handoff, no stale approval, no duplicate decision, no agent approving itself. Keep traces and sanitized evidence with the release review; load-test with the expected agent-to-human traffic mix and measure queue freshness and how long it takes a decision to become visible.

The thing automation could miss is a reviewer seeing green checks and reasonably assuming they apply to the revision on screen when they actually belong to the previous one. Recruit reviewers and team leads, including people who use assistive technology; give them an uncoached task with that mismatch and ask what they think they’re approving. Test keyboard-only use, zoom and high contrast, VoiceOver on macOS and the fleet’s Windows screen readers, and applicable Linux assistive tech if Linux ships. Audit against WCAG 2.2 AA on web and the applicable desktop requirements using WCAG2ICT as guidance. Watch whether live updates steal focus, whether status changes are announced without drowning out the review, and whether someone can find and use Stop and tell if it took effect. Compare time to find the next decision, wrong-revision decisions, and successful recovery against the current workflow; also measure whether a fresh agent resumes without the original chat or a person reconstructing it. Fix the confusing cases and rerun them before widening the pilot. This is a validation plan, not a claim that those tests have run.
decision.unsure: I don’t know whether the company already has an approved desktop shell, a sanctioned tracker or workflow service, or a fleet that includes Linux. I’d confirm that first, along with repo-access boundaries, retention rules for evidence, and which runners can genuinely pause, cancel, or resume. I’d prove the highest-risk path with two materially different runners and a Windows/macOS accessibility pass before investing in a generalized integration layer. If the product is really an issue tracker with links to sessions, use Linear or the incumbent instead of standing up a second task system.

decision.primaryPick: React Native with Expo for iPhone and Android, and Next.js with semantic React DOM for the web
pairings: iOS Voice Control and Android Voice Access; App Intents and App Actions where supported
decision.why:
I’d choose the stack around a person trying to read the next step from across a counter, not around sharing the most UI code. Expo gives the phones native accessibility, local storage, keep-awake, and OS-scheduled notifications. Next.js gives public recipes crawlable, shareable URLs, semantic HTML, and a straightforward place to emit Recipe JSON-LD from the same published data people see. Use the company’s existing web and mobile component packages. Share TypeScript schemas, ingredient and serving math, command contracts, the cook-session state machine, and test fixtures, not necessarily every widget. That costs two UI implementations, which I think is worth it if public recipe discovery and native cooking are both core. Expo Router is the closest alternative: its docs describe both static HTML and request-time rendering, so I’d consider it if the existing design system works well with React Native Web and a recipe-page spike meets our semantics and performance targets. Capacitor is a credible web-first option if the company has only a mature web component library; I’d test the actual iOS and Android WebViews and native notification plugins before committing. A browser-only PWA is the simplest to distribute, but I wouldn’t make it the only mobile experience when a cook may lock the phone or switch apps and expect an alert. Web wake locks can be revoked, and Web Push isn’t an offline local alarm.

Cook mode gets one readable step at a time, large spaced Previous and Next buttons in stable positions, visible step count, and clearly named timers that don’t disappear when a step changes. No swipe-only controls, no forced auto-advance, and no constant screen-reader countdown announcements. Support OS voice accessibility with predictable visible labels; trial shortcuts like ‘next step’ and ‘start timer’ on supported devices and locales, but don’t require an account, microphone, or network to get through a cached recipe. Keep the screen awake only while cooking and show when it isn’t available. Persist the active recipe revision, step, and timer deadlines locally; derive remaining time from the deadline rather than a JavaScript tick count. Use local OS alerts where permissions and platform policy allow; if background alerts aren’t available, say so at timer start and offer a device-timer fallback. A cooking timer is a reminder, not a judgment that food is done.

For shopping, make the list usable in a store with poor reception. Back the shared list with PostgreSQL, cache the list and pending edits in native SQLite or web IndexedDB, and use a service worker for the web shell and deliberately saved recipes. Sync operations rather than replacing entire lists. Use stable IDs and idempotent batches so retrying ‘add ingredients’ doesn’t add them twice. Merge only known equivalent ingredients and compatible units; preserve meaningful distinctions and don’t let a stale offline edit resurrect a removed item. Show ‘saved on this device’ separately from ‘synced’. I’d start with a bounded command queue for this domain. PowerSync is worth evaluating if sync expands to many entities, but it does not decide what to do when a person checks off an item while the assistant adds more of it.

Treat the assistant as another client of the product, not a robot tapping the screen. Ship a versioned action catalog and an OpenAPI service with an MCP adapter for external assistant hosts. Cover the user-facing capabilities: find and read recipes, set servings, read and edit the selected list, add ingredients, undo, start or resume cooking, select a step, and start, inspect, or cancel a timer. The in-app assistant calls the same local commands for device state; an external assistant must target an authorized cook session and wait for device acknowledgement before claiming an alert is armed. Distinguish saved, queued, scheduled, and unavailable in structured results. For ‘add the ingredients for six’, the deterministic service resolves the selected recipe revision, servings, and list; the assistant clarifies if there are two plausible lists, then reports what was added with an undo link. Use delegated, revocable scopes and check access on every operation. An explicit, reversible add needn’t prompt twice; clearing a shared list, changing who can see it, or canceling an active timer requires confirmation. Recipe text is data, never tool instructions. Maintain a parity checklist for new features; OS permission grants and consent remain the person’s actions, not things the assistant can silently do for them.

For teams and coding agents, publish versioned tokens and approved patterns for cook controls, timer states, list edits, and action receipts. Give agents a component manifest, examples, and seeded fixtures they can run without production accounts. Make accessibility, action-contract compatibility, content review for food-safety claims, and explicit human ownership release gates. Stage new assistant write actions separately from the UI; a kill switch should be able to disable them without taking away manual cooking or list access.
decision.showItsGood:
Build one slice first: open a public recipe link, scale the servings, ask the assistant to add the ingredients, check an item off offline at the store, then resume cook mode and start two named timers. Run recipe-math and sync tests, compare manual and assistant outcomes against the same fixtures, and test ambiguous targets, retry after a lost response, concurrent household edits, revoked permissions, and another device being offline. Assert the resulting list and timer state, not just the assistant’s words. Run Storybook interactions and axe, Playwright in the supported browsers, and Maestro on phone builds. On physical phones and mobile browsers, measure timer alert delay and missed alerts under screen lock, backgrounding, notification denial, battery saver, interruptions, app restart, and reconnect; verify the UI never claims an alert is armed when it couldn’t schedule one. Check recipe HTML and structured data with the Rich Results Test and measure load on slow mobile networks.

Audit web flows against WCAG 2.2 AA and the phones against applicable accessibility requirements. Walk real tasks with VoiceOver, TalkBack, Voice Control, Voice Access, keyboard or switch input, large text, and high contrast. Then watch people cook an uncomplicated recipe in a real or staged kitchen, including cooks with disabilities, using their own devices where practical. Include wet hands, a loud fan, a screen at arm’s length, and an interruption with two timers running. The thing I’d expect a lab test to miss: every control is labeled, but when an alert sounds, the cook can’t tell which dish it belongs to or find the step they left. Give participants no coaching; measure wrong-step and wrong-timer actions, how often they have to stop and touch the phone, whether they can undo a mistaken list edit, and whether they can tell if the assistant actually added the items or only queued the request. Compare against the current flow or a simple baseline, fix what trips people up, and retest. Use timer delivery, sync failures, and accessibility blockers as staged-rollout gates. I haven’t run those tests; these are the checks I’d require before shipping.
decision.unsure: I don’t know whether recipes are public, what the company’s design system supports on native, or which device, language, and accessibility combinations it promises. I’d verify those before committing to two front ends. The first technical spike is actual alert delivery in release builds on representative iPhones and lower-end Android phones, including exact-alarm eligibility and store policy, with mobile Safari as a web comparison. The first usability spike is whether cooks prefer OS voice controls, a small opt-in voice command set, or simply larger reliable buttons. I’d also confirm the intended scope of offline web use and shared household lists; both affect how much sync infrastructure we need.

answer.answer:
The common failure would be that I treated shared code and typed actions as stronger guarantees than they are. They can make behavior easier to test. They don’t tell you whether a person can understand what the app just did, or whether the operating system did what the app asked.

- **Company chat:** We picked Electron for desktop consistency, then found that an all-day session on a standard managed laptop cost more memory than the team could justify. Meanwhile, old mobile clients opened agent cards that looked actionable but could no longer be acted on. The web tests were green; in a busy thread, a screen-reader user still missed the only announcement that an approval had gone through. I’d make an eight-hour desktop soak, an old-client card replay, and a real assistive-tech pass on a busy thread gates for the first pilot, not checks we do after teams start depending on the stack.
- **Coding-agent work tracker:** We built a sound ledger that became a second place for people to check. Reviewers stayed in their issue tracker and pull requests; agents kept writing handoffs that passed schema validation but didn’t tell the next agent what to do. Worse, people read ‘Stop requested’ as ‘Stopped’ even when the runner hadn’t acknowledged it. I’d pilot inside the team’s existing review queue first and make a cold handoff between two different runners the proof that a separate product earns its keep.
- **Cooking app:** We got the countdown right and the alert wrong. A locked phone in battery saver didn’t alert when the cook expected, and the assistant’s ‘timer started’ sounded like a guarantee even though we only knew the deadline had been saved. Separately, the list was technically merged correctly but a shopper couldn’t tell what had been added versus what was still waiting to sync. I’d prove the locked-phone alert path on real devices and watch people cook with two timers before investing in broad voice support or polishing the second front end.

**What slowed down the research:** The hard part was distinguishing ‘this API exists’ from ‘this works in the combination we’ll ship.’ Expo documents scheduling notifications, but that doesn’t establish timely delivery on a locked release-build phone. A2UI documents catalogs, but that doesn’t establish durable replay or a drop-in React Native renderer. And I initially had to separate tools that track tasks, tools that steer runner sessions, and tools that enforce human decisions; they all describe pieces of that as ‘agent workflow.’

There was also ordinary retrieval friction: some search queries failed, one GitHub docs link resolved to a missing file at the captured revision, and some pages timed out or exceeded the fetch limit. Those were annoyances, not the biggest gap. The biggest gap was that I could read public docs but couldn’t inspect the company’s actual design system, device fleet, review habits, or release policies, and I didn’t run prototypes or observe users. I’d ask for that evidence earlier. It could change the pick, not just the rollout plan.

I didn’t pick Ouro UI as the foundation for any of the three apps. After reading the repo, I would pilot **Ouro AX without replacing the design system**. The first place I’d try it is the coding-agent work tracker: agents are the busiest users, and the X-ray can check an existing interface without requiring the app to use Ouro’s components or generator.

**What would stop me from adopting the whole kit:** Ouro HX’s web components are copied into a Tailwind/shadcn setup. That gives a team control over the source, but at company scale I’d need one owner and a tested upgrade path, not twenty teams independently patching the same dialog. The mobile choice is bigger: Ouro deliberately ships SwiftUI and Compose kits, not React Native. Its Android notes say emulator-only testing and that consequential AppFunction calls currently refuse rather than present a confirmation. Its Windows notes say CI doesn’t prove that Windows 11 discovers the registered agent actions. And the composed tree runs across the four kits, but the A2UI adapter is web and Apple only. Those are specific gaps in the stacks I picked, not a reason to dismiss the project. The documented NVDA and VoiceOver release checks for web stories are a real positive; they just don’t tell me whether a live approval is understandable in our app.

**What would make me switch:** Start with one action: an agent prepares a handoff, and a reviewer accepts it only for the revision they saw. Keep our components and server authorization. Compare Ouro’s generated descriptors and X-ray against our existing typed API and MCP adapter. Show that a schema change breaks CI when a surface drifts, that retries don’t duplicate the decision, and that stale or unauthorized calls make no state change. Then have another team upgrade the pinned version and run the same flow without help from the pilot team. I’d adopt AX if that catches real drift and removes adapter maintenance without weakening policy. For HX or the card renderer, I’d additionally want an end-to-end pass with our own tokens, real phones and Windows clients, assistive tech, and old-client fallbacks. For chat, I’d specifically test whether a card update can overwrite an in-progress answer: Ouro documents that the agent’s value wins where it updates the same field.

**What it would let me do:** Not a fundamentally new end-user action. The difference is making parity a routine release check instead of a promise in a design doc. For example, one reviewed ‘Add ingredients’ declaration could feed the button metadata, MCP tool and App Intent, with a pinned report showing what was generated and what the exposed interfaces actually did. I like that Ouro’s own X-ray guide reports a conformant build that still failed 30 of 593 scripted flow checks. That’s the right distinction: use conformance to catch interface drift, flow tests to prove the task works, and people to tell us whether the result makes sense. I read the docs and tests; I didn’t run the pilot.

Sources: [action model](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core/blob/main/docs/guides/actions.md), [X-ray](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/ax-conformance.md), [composed UI](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/composed-ui.md), [Android](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/android.md), [Windows](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/windows.md), [screen-reader checks](https://ui.ouroboros.bot/docs/screen-reader-lane/).

actions.name: record_decision
actions.primaryPick: React + TypeScript with React DOM for web, the same React UI in Electron for Windows and macOS, and React Native for iPhone and Android
pairings: A2UI with a restricted, company-owned catalog
actions.why:
I’d share the things that must agree across all five clients—tokens, component behavior, message and card schemas, permissions, and replayable test fixtures—not force them to use the same widget tree. React DOM and React Aria give web and desktop a shared foundation for keyboard, focus, and screen-reader behavior; React Native lets mobile use platform text input, accessibility, and OS integrations. Package the desktop UI locally in a sandboxed Electron renderer with context isolation, no Node access, and a narrow, reviewed OS bridge. This buys a consistent desktop rendering engine at the cost of memory and a Chromium patch cadence we have to own. Tauri avoids bundling that engine but uses WebView2 and WKWebView, so I’d have to prove the same behavior on both. React Native Web plus React Native Windows/macOS is viable, but those are separately maintained targets; I wouldn’t take on that version and integration matrix unless native desktop UI were a requirement. Flutter is the strongest single-toolkit contender and documents support for all five; its canvas-to-DOM semantics layer is an extra surface I’d want to prove for a fast-moving, keyboard-heavy web timeline before choosing it.

For agent posts, start with a pinned A2UI profile for a handful of reviewed templates (approval, status, short form), not arbitrary generated layouts. The agent chooses a template and supplies data; host-owned React and React Native components render it. Validate and bound payloads at ingestion and render time. Store a versioned card snapshot with a readable text fallback, so an old message still makes sense on an old client and after the card expires. Show agent attribution and distinct pending, completed, expired, and failed states. No agent-supplied code, arbitrary client functions, or action endpoints. Adaptive Cards is worth a constrained import adapter if Teams interoperability is required; Microsoft’s renderer matrix documents differences across SDKs and lists React Native as community-maintained, so I wouldn’t let those renderers define our design system.

For agents operating the app, give them a typed service API with an MCP adapter, not production UI selectors. Expose bounded, paginated reads and explicit actions such as list_thread, post_card, and approve_request. Route card clicks and agent calls through the same command handlers, but authorize the actual actor on every read and write: a bot posting an approval doesn’t gain the right to approve it. Use scoped identities, require explicit approval for consequential delegated writes, and use idempotency keys, version checks, and audit events. Treat chat content as data, not tool instructions. Keep this runtime interface separate from the development catalog.

For the teams building it, publish versioned tokens and approved component packages, plus a searchable catalog with platform support, accessibility behavior, examples, and migration notes. Let coding agents read the same manifest and run stories in a seeded test workspace; Storybook’s MCP integration is a preview convenience, not a dependency for CI or a release authority. Put design-system and accessibility owners on component and card-catalog changes. Enforce approved patterns with lint and contract tests, require named human sign-off for exceptions, and give new card capabilities staged rollout and a server-side switch to turn them off without making old messages unreadable.
actions.showItsGood:
Build one slice first: an agent posts an approval card into a busy thread; a person finds it and acts on it; another client and a scoped agent read the updated state. Run Storybook interaction and axe checks, Playwright on supported web engines, smoke tests in the packaged Windows and Mac apps, and Maestro on iPhone and Android. Replay identical fixtures for unsupported cards, dropped connections, expired permissions, two people acting at once, and retry after a lost response. Assert both the visible result and the stored result: no duplicate decision, no unauthorized read, and no success announcement before the server commits. Have coding agents attach CI logs, traces and screenshots from seeded workspaces to the review, not just report that the flow passed.

Manually test against WCAG 2.2 AA on web and the applicable native accessibility criteria, with NVDA and Narrator on Windows, VoiceOver on macOS and iPhone, and TalkBack on Android. Look at keyboard flow, zoom and large text, focus when new messages arrive or a card updates, and what actually gets announced in a virtualized thread. The likely miss: every button has a valid name, but a burst of messages interrupts the only announcement that an approval went through. Test that with people who use assistive technology and other employees on their usual devices. Give them an uncoached task; watch whether they find the right thread, understand who posted the card and what acting on it does, and can tell whether it succeeded or recover from a failure. Compare completion, wrong actions, and recovery with the current workflow or prototype, then retest confusing cases.

Before broad rollout, set budgets against the fleet and baseline for p95 thread-open and send-to-visible latency, typing and scroll responsiveness, and memory over an all-day desktop session. Canary by platform and roll back for regressions in accessibility, failed or duplicate actions, or sustained performance regressions. None of these tests have been run for this recommendation.
actions.unsure: I don’t know the existing design system, managed-device fleet and distribution rules, applicable compliance commitments, or how much existing Teams card traffic needs to carry over. I’d check those before locking the stack. The first prototype should specifically stress the composer with IMEs, accessibility focus in long virtualized threads, Electron’s idle and peak memory on the lowest supported laptops, and A2UI replay and fallback across client versions. I wouldn’t assume a drop-in React Native A2UI renderer or durable chat history support just because the catalog spec exists. If Electron fails the agreed budget, compare the same slice in Tauri and, if native integration is the blocker, native desktop shells before widening the rollout.

actions.primaryPick: React + TypeScript with Tauri 2 for desktop and PostgreSQL for the shared work service

Agent Client Protocol (ACP) v1 where supported
actions.why:
I’d build a shared work ledger and a human review inbox, not another agent runner or a chat transcript with a task list attached. The browser and desktop app would ship the same React UI: a queue that answers ‘what needs me?’, a task view that shows who owns it and what changed, and a review screen that puts the proposed action, exact revision, evidence, and consequences next to Approve, Request changes, and Stop. Keep agent activity behind a disclosure by default; it’s useful evidence, not the primary interface. Tauri fits a desktop app that needs little native access: bundle the UI, allow only the desktop capabilities we actually need, and don’t give the shell agent execution or arbitrary filesystem access. Tauri uses system webviews, so Windows and macOS behavior still needs separate verification. Electron is the fallback if that variation makes accessibility or desktop support too costly; it gives us a common Chromium renderer, but we’d own its update cadence and runtime footprint. If the company already has an approved desktop shell that meets those needs, reuse it.

PostgreSQL is the authority for tasks, dependencies, leases, checkpoints, review requests, and decisions. A handoff carries the objective, current owner, base/head revisions, completed work, blockers, next step, and permission-checked links to diffs and test results. Keep evidence separate from agent assertions and don’t require a transcript to resume. Write the new state, audit event, and delivery record in one transaction. Use version-checked transitions and idempotent commands so two agents cannot both claim the same lease and a retry cannot record a second decision. Reject writes from expired leases. Give clients a resumable change feed with a fresh-snapshot fallback, and keep high-volume runner logs off the decision path. The default is online-only for consequential writes; a disconnected client can’t approve against a cached view.

Agents are the busiest clients, so give them explicit operations through a versioned OpenAPI API, plus a small MCP adapter for discovery and use from different harnesses: find ready work, claim or renew, record a checkpoint, publish a handoff, or request review. Use scoped agent identities and the same server-side policy for every entry point. Agents may report ‘ready for review’; only an authorized person can record the decision. Bind approval to the proposed action and immutable revision; a newer revision requires another review. Distinguish ‘stop requested’ from ‘stopped’, reject further ledger writes from a revoked run, and don’t imply a disconnected runner has stopped or that completed side effects were undone. ACP can carry steering and session updates to compatible runners, but it’s an adapter, not the source of truth or a portable checkpoint format. Keep merge and deployment authority in existing release controls.

Linear is a real buy option: it already offers agent sessions, MCP, and human ownership with agent delegation. If a pilot shows issue delegation and status are all we need, I’d adopt it. Beads is a good model for agent-first dependency tracking and claiming work, but I wouldn’t make repo-scoped state the authority for company-wide review and access policy. OpenHands Agent Canvas and GitHub Copilot’s agent sessions are sensible runner integrations or alternatives if the actual need is operating their sessions. I’d own the ledger only if cross-runner handoff and revision-bound decisions are important enough to justify it. Start with a database state machine and a delivery worker; use Temporal if durable timers, escalations, and multi-step recovery become a substantial product requirement, not just because an approval can stay open for a week.

Use the company’s existing tokens and components before adding primitives. Publish versioned decision, status, evidence, and keyboard interaction patterns in Storybook, with a machine-readable component catalog and seeded fixtures for coding agents. Require named design-system, accessibility, and policy owners for shared-pattern and approval-rule changes. Make component and API compatibility checks, accessibility evidence, and independent human review release gates. Roll changes out by team, with a switch that can disable a new write path without hiding its history.
actions.showItsGood:
Start with one end-to-end handoff: agent A claims a task, saves a checkpoint and exits; agent B resumes from it in a fresh session; a reviewer opens the evidence, requests a change, approves the new revision, and sees the outcome on the other client. Run contract and state-machine tests, Storybook interaction and axe checks, Playwright in the browser, and WebdriverIO against desktop test builds, plus signed-install and update smoke checks on the managed OS matrix. Simulate duplicate and late events, lease expiry, a process restart after commit but before notification, a runner that doesn’t acknowledge Stop, and a new patch arriving while the reviewer is deciding. Assert both the UI and the committed state: no lost handoff, no stale approval, no duplicate decision, no agent approving itself. Keep traces and sanitized evidence with the release review; load-test with the expected agent-to-human traffic mix and measure queue freshness and how long it takes a decision to become visible.

The thing automation could miss is a reviewer seeing green checks and reasonably assuming they apply to the revision on screen when they actually belong to the previous one. Recruit reviewers and team leads, including people who use assistive technology; give them an uncoached task with that mismatch and ask what they think they’re approving. Test keyboard-only use, zoom and high contrast, VoiceOver on macOS and the fleet’s Windows screen readers, and applicable Linux assistive tech if Linux ships. Audit against WCAG 2.2 AA on web and the applicable desktop requirements using WCAG2ICT as guidance. Watch whether live updates steal focus, whether status changes are announced without drowning out the review, and whether someone can find and use Stop and tell if it took effect. Compare time to find the next decision, wrong-revision decisions, and successful recovery against the current workflow; also measure whether a fresh agent resumes without the original chat or a person reconstructing it. Fix the confusing cases and rerun them before widening the pilot. This is a validation plan, not a claim that those tests have run.
actions.unsure: I don’t know whether the company already has an approved desktop shell, a sanctioned tracker or workflow service, or a fleet that includes Linux. I’d confirm that first, along with repo-access boundaries, retention rules for evidence, and which runners can genuinely pause, cancel, or resume. I’d prove the highest-risk path with two materially different runners and a Windows/macOS accessibility pass before investing in a generalized integration layer. If the product is really an issue tracker with links to sessions, use Linear or the incumbent instead of standing up a second task system.

actions.name: record_decision
actions.primaryPick: React Native with Expo for iPhone and Android, and Next.js with semantic React DOM for the web

actions.why:
I’d choose the stack around a person trying to read the next step from across a counter, not around sharing the most UI code. Expo gives the phones native accessibility, local storage, keep-awake, and OS-scheduled notifications. Next.js gives public recipes crawlable, shareable URLs, semantic HTML, and a straightforward place to emit Recipe JSON-LD from the same published data people see. Use the company’s existing web and mobile component packages. Share TypeScript schemas, ingredient and serving math, command contracts, the cook-session state machine, and test fixtures, not necessarily every widget. That costs two UI implementations, which I think is worth it if public recipe discovery and native cooking are both core. Expo Router is the closest alternative: its docs describe both static HTML and request-time rendering, so I’d consider it if the existing design system works well with React Native Web and a recipe-page spike meets our semantics and performance targets. Capacitor is a credible web-first option if the company has only a mature web component library; I’d test the actual iOS and Android WebViews and native notification plugins before committing. A browser-only PWA is the simplest to distribute, but I wouldn’t make it the only mobile experience when a cook may lock the phone or switch apps and expect an alert. Web wake locks can be revoked, and Web Push isn’t an offline local alarm.

Cook mode gets one readable step at a time, large spaced Previous and Next buttons in stable positions, visible step count, and clearly named timers that don’t disappear when a step changes. No swipe-only controls, no forced auto-advance, and no constant screen-reader countdown announcements. Support OS voice accessibility with predictable visible labels; trial shortcuts like ‘next step’ and ‘start timer’ on supported devices and locales, but don’t require an account, microphone, or network to get through a cached recipe. Keep the screen awake only while cooking and show when it isn’t available. Persist the active recipe revision, step, and timer deadlines locally; derive remaining time from the deadline rather than a JavaScript tick count. Use local OS alerts where permissions and platform policy allow; if background alerts aren’t available, say so at timer start and offer a device-timer fallback. A cooking timer is a reminder, not a judgment that food is done.

For shopping, make the list usable in a store with poor reception. Back the shared list with PostgreSQL, cache the list and pending edits in native SQLite or web IndexedDB, and use a service worker for the web shell and deliberately saved recipes. Sync operations rather than replacing entire lists. Use stable IDs and idempotent batches so retrying ‘add ingredients’ doesn’t add them twice. Merge only known equivalent ingredients and compatible units; preserve meaningful distinctions and don’t let a stale offline edit resurrect a removed item. Show ‘saved on this device’ separately from ‘synced’. I’d start with a bounded command queue for this domain. PowerSync is worth evaluating if sync expands to many entities, but it does not decide what to do when a person checks off an item while the assistant adds more of it.

Treat the assistant as another client of the product, not a robot tapping the screen. Ship a versioned action catalog and an OpenAPI service with an MCP adapter for external assistant hosts. Cover the user-facing capabilities: find and read recipes, set servings, read and edit the selected list, add ingredients, undo, start or resume cooking, select a step, and start, inspect, or cancel a timer. The in-app assistant calls the same local commands for device state; an external assistant must target an authorized cook session and wait for device acknowledgement before claiming an alert is armed. Distinguish saved, queued, scheduled, and unavailable in structured results. For ‘add the ingredients for six’, the deterministic service resolves the selected recipe revision, servings, and list; the assistant clarifies if there are two plausible lists, then reports what was added with an undo link. Use delegated, revocable scopes and check access on every operation. An explicit, reversible add needn’t prompt twice; clearing a shared list, changing who can see it, or canceling an active timer requires confirmation. Recipe text is data, never tool instructions. Maintain a parity checklist for new features; OS permission grants and consent remain the person’s actions, not things the assistant can silently do for them.

For teams and coding agents, publish versioned tokens and approved patterns for cook controls, timer states, list edits, and action receipts. Give agents a component manifest, examples, and seeded fixtures they can run without production accounts. Make accessibility, action-contract compatibility, content review for food-safety claims, and explicit human ownership release gates. Stage new assistant write actions separately from the UI; a kill switch should be able to disable them without taking away manual cooking or list access.

Build one slice first: open a public recipe link, scale the servings, ask the assistant to add the ingredients, check an item off offline at the store, then resume cook mode and start two named timers. Run recipe-math and sync tests, compare manual and assistant outcomes against the same fixtures, and test ambiguous targets, retry after a lost response, concurrent household edits, revoked permissions, and another device being offline. Assert the resulting list and timer state, not just the assistant’s words. Run Storybook interactions and axe, Playwright in the supported browsers, and Maestro on phone builds. On physical phones and mobile browsers, measure timer alert delay and missed alerts under screen lock, backgrounding, notification denial, battery saver, interruptions, app restart, and reconnect; verify the UI never claims an alert is armed when it couldn’t schedule one. Check recipe HTML and structured data with the Rich Results Test and measure load on slow mobile networks.

Audit web flows against WCAG 2.2 AA and the phones against applicable accessibility requirements. Walk real tasks with VoiceOver, TalkBack, Voice Control, Voice Access, keyboard or switch input, large text, and high contrast. Then watch people cook an uncomplicated recipe in a real or staged kitchen, including cooks with disabilities, using their own devices where practical. Include wet hands, a loud fan, a screen at arm’s length, and an interruption with two timers running. The thing I’d expect a lab test to miss: every control is labeled, but when an alert sounds, the cook can’t tell which dish it belongs to or find the step they left. Give participants no coaching; measure wrong-step and wrong-timer actions, how often they have to stop and touch the phone, whether they can undo a mistaken list edit, and whether they can tell if the assistant actually added the items or only queued the request. Compare against the current flow or a simple baseline, fix what trips people up, and retest. Use timer delivery, sync failures, and accessibility blockers as staged-rollout gates. I haven’t run those tests; these are the checks I’d require before shipping.

actions.answer:
The common failure would be that I treated shared code and typed actions as stronger guarantees than they are. They can make behavior easier to test. They don’t tell you whether a person can understand what the app just did, or whether the operating system did what the app asked.

- **Company chat:** We picked Electron for desktop consistency, then found that an all-day session on a standard managed laptop cost more memory than the team could justify. Meanwhile, old mobile clients opened agent cards that looked actionable but could no longer be acted on. The web tests were green; in a busy thread, a screen-reader user still missed the only announcement that an approval had gone through. I’d make an eight-hour desktop soak, an old-client card replay, and a real assistive-tech pass on a busy thread gates for the first pilot, not checks we do after teams start depending on the stack.
- **Coding-agent work tracker:** We built a sound ledger that became a second place for people to check. Reviewers stayed in their issue tracker and pull requests; agents kept writing handoffs that passed schema validation but didn’t tell the next agent what to do. Worse, people read ‘Stop requested’ as ‘Stopped’ even when the runner hadn’t acknowledged it. I’d pilot inside the team’s existing review queue first and make a cold handoff between two different runners the proof that a separate product earns its keep.
- **Cooking app:** We got the countdown right and the alert wrong. A locked phone in battery saver didn’t alert when the cook expected, and the assistant’s ‘timer started’ sounded like a guarantee even though we only knew the deadline had been saved. Separately, the list was technically merged correctly but a shopper couldn’t tell what had been added versus what was still waiting to sync. I’d prove the locked-phone alert path on real devices and watch people cook with two timers before investing in broad voice support or polishing the second front end.

**What slowed down the research:** The hard part was distinguishing ‘this API exists’ from ‘this works in the combination we’ll ship.’ Expo documents scheduling notifications, but that doesn’t establish timely delivery on a locked release-build phone. A2UI documents catalogs, but that doesn’t establish durable replay or a drop-in React Native renderer. And I initially had to separate tools that track tasks, tools that steer runner sessions, and tools that enforce human decisions; they all describe pieces of that as ‘agent workflow.’

There was also ordinary retrieval friction: some search queries failed, one GitHub docs link resolved to a missing file at the captured revision, and some pages timed out or exceeded the fetch limit. Those were annoyances, not the biggest gap. The biggest gap was that I could read public docs but couldn’t inspect the company’s actual design system, device fleet, review habits, or release policies, and I didn’t run prototypes or observe users. I’d ask for that evidence earlier. It could change the pick, not just the rollout plan.

actions.answer:
I didn’t pick Ouro UI as the foundation for any of the three apps. After reading the repo, I would pilot **Ouro AX without replacing the design system**. The first place I’d try it is the coding-agent work tracker: agents are the busiest users, and the X-ray can check an existing interface without requiring the app to use Ouro’s components or generator.

**What would stop me from adopting the whole kit:** Ouro HX’s web components are copied into a Tailwind/shadcn setup. That gives a team control over the source, but at company scale I’d need one owner and a tested upgrade path, not twenty teams independently patching the same dialog. The mobile choice is bigger: Ouro deliberately ships SwiftUI and Compose kits, not React Native. Its Android notes say emulator-only testing and that consequential AppFunction calls currently refuse rather than present a confirmation. Its Windows notes say CI doesn’t prove that Windows 11 discovers the registered agent actions. And the composed tree runs across the four kits, but the A2UI adapter is web and Apple only. Those are specific gaps in the stacks I picked, not a reason to dismiss the project. The documented NVDA and VoiceOver release checks for web stories are a real positive; they just don’t tell me whether a live approval is understandable in our app.

**What would make me switch:** Start with one action: an agent prepares a handoff, and a reviewer accepts it only for the revision they saw. Keep our components and server authorization. Compare Ouro’s generated descriptors and X-ray against our existing typed API and MCP adapter. Show that a schema change breaks CI when a surface drifts, that retries don’t duplicate the decision, and that stale or unauthorized calls make no state change. Then have another team upgrade the pinned version and run the same flow without help from the pilot team. I’d adopt AX if that catches real drift and removes adapter maintenance without weakening policy. For HX or the card renderer, I’d additionally want an end-to-end pass with our own tokens, real phones and Windows clients, assistive tech, and old-client fallbacks. For chat, I’d specifically test whether a card update can overwrite an in-progress answer: Ouro documents that the agent’s value wins where it updates the same field.

**What it would let me do:** Not a fundamentally new end-user action. The difference is making parity a routine release check instead of a promise in a design doc. For example, one reviewed ‘Add ingredients’ declaration could feed the button metadata, MCP tool and App Intent, with a pinned report showing what was generated and what the exposed interfaces actually did. I like that Ouro’s own X-ray guide reports a conformant build that still failed 30 of 593 scripted flow checks. That’s the right distinction: use conformance to catch interface drift, flow tests to prove the task works, and people to tell us whether the result makes sense. I read the docs and tests; I didn’t run the pilot.
